14. Optimization & Machine Learning: Smooth Optimization

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Training a model often reduces to minimizing a differentiable objective, so the geometry of that objective determines how optimization algorithms progress. Starting from regression and classification, we develop convexity, derivatives, and optimality conditions, then derive gradient descent and practical step-size rules. Quadratic examples guide the convergence analysis, which extends to smooth convex objectives and explains the effects of conditioning, strong convexity, and acceleration.

14.1 Motivation in Machine Learning¶

14.1.1 Unconstrained Optimization¶

Throughout most of this chapter, we consider unconstrained convex optimization problems of the form

inf⁡x∈Rp  f(x),(14.1)\underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\inf}\; f(x), \tag{14.1}x∈Rpinf​f(x),(14.1)

and seek algorithms that approximate a minimizer, when one exists, with a low cost per iteration.

The first-order methods studied here use gradient information. We write

argminx  f(x):={x∈Rp  ;  f(x)=inf⁡f},\underset{x}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; f(x) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^p \;;\; f(x) = \inf{f} \right\} ,xargmin​f(x):={x∈Rp;f(x)=inff},

for the set of minimizers of fff, which may contain several points or be empty: argminf=∅\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}f = \emptysetargminf=∅. When a minimizer exists, we write the optimization problem as

min⁡x∈Rp  f(x).(14.2)\underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\min}\; f(x). \tag{14.2}x∈Rpmin​f(x).(14.2)

In learning, f(x)f(x)f(x) is typically an empirical risk for regression or classification, and ppp is the number of model parameters. For a linear model, the training sample is (ai,yi)i=1n(a_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n(ai​,yi​)i=1n​ with feature vectors ai∈Rpa_i \in \mathbb{R}^pai​∈Rp.

14.2 Basics of Convex Analysis¶

14.2.1 Existence of Solutions¶

Problem (14.1) need not have a minimizer. An objective fff may be unbounded below: for f(x)=−x2f(x)=-x^2f(x)=−x2, the infimum is −∞-\infty−∞. The objective fff can also have a finite unattained infimum: for f(x)=e−xf(x)=e^{-x}f(x)=e−x, it is inf⁡f=0\inf f=0inff=0.

Figure 14.2. Left: no minimizer. Middle: multiple minimizers. Right: a unique minimizer.

A continuous function attains its minimum on a nonempty compact set Ω⊂Rp\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^pΩ⊂Rp. In finite dimensions, compactness means that Ω\OmegaΩ is closed and bounded. Lower semicontinuity suffices for attainment, but we use continuity here. For unconstrained minimization, coercivity provides a compact set to which the search can be restricted: f(x)→+∞f(x) \rightarrow +\inftyf(x)→+∞ as ∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣→+∞|\!| x |\!|\rightarrow+\infty∣∣x∣∣→+∞. For any x0∈Rpx_0 \in \mathbb{R}^px0​∈Rp, consider the sublevel set

Ω={x∈Rp  ;  f(x)⩽f(x0)}\Omega= \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^p \;;\; f(x) \leqslant f(x_0) \right\}Ω={x∈Rp;f(x)⩽f(x0​)}

Coercivity makes this set bounded, and continuity of fff makes it closed. For a continuous convex function, coercivity is in fact equivalent to a nonempty bounded minimizer set. Convexity matters: f(x)=min⁡(1,x2)f(x)=\min(1,x^2)f(x)=min(1,x2) has a unique minimizer but is not coercive.

Figure 14.3. Coercivity condition for least squares.

Example 14.1 (Least squares)

The least-squares objective f(x)=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y∣ ⁣∣2f(x)=\frac{1}{2}|\!| Ax-y |\!|^2f(x)=21​∣∣Ax−y∣∣2 is coercive exactly when ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A)=\{0\}ker(A)={0}, meaning the design has full column rank. If ker⁡(A)≠{0}\ker(A) \neq \{0\}ker(A)={0} and x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a minimizer, then x⋆+ux^\star+ux⋆+u is also a minimizer for every u∈ker⁡(A)u \in \ker(A)u∈ker(A), so the minimizer set is unbounded.

Conversely, if ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A) = \{0\}ker(A)={0}, we will show later that the minimizer is unique, see Fig. 14.3.

For classification, strict convexity of ℓ\ellℓ and injectivity of AAA imply strict convexity of the objective, but do not ensure coercivity or existence. Separable logistic regression is a counterexample.

14.2.2 Convexity¶

Convexity is central to optimization because every local minimizer is global, and many convex problems admit efficient algorithms. A function is convex if, for every pair (x,y)∈(Rp)2(x,y) \in (\mathbb{R}^p)^2(x,y)∈(Rp)2,

∀ t∈[0,1],f((1−t)x+ty)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)(14.5)\forall \,t \in [0,1], \quad f((1-t)x + t y) \leqslant(1-t)f(x) + t f(y) \tag{14.5}∀t∈[0,1],f((1−t)x+ty)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)(14.5)

The graph lies below each secant, and above each tangent when differentiable; see Figure 14.4.

If x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a local minimizer of a convex fff, then x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a global minimizer, i.e. x⋆∈argminfx^\star \in \mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}fx⋆∈argminf.

Convexity is preserved by several useful operations. If fff and ggg are convex and a,ba, ba,b are positive, then af+bga f + b gaf+bg and max⁡(f,g)\max(f,g)max(f,g) are convex. If g:Rq→Rg : \mathbb{R}^q \rightarrow \mathbb{R}g:Rq→R is convex and B∈Rq×p,b∈RqB \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}, b \in \mathbb{R}^qB∈Rq×p,b∈Rq, then the affine composition f(x)=g(Bx+b)f(x) = g(B x+b)f(x)=g(Bx+b) is convex.

Thus the squared loss (14.3) is convex, since ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣2/2|\!| \cdot |\!|^2/2∣∣⋅∣∣2/2 is a sum of convex squares.

Similarly, convexity of ℓ\ellℓ implies convexity of LLL and of the classification objective (14.4).

Strict convexity.

When fff is convex, one can strengthen the condition (14.5) and impose that the inequality is strict for distinct x,yx,yx,y and t∈]0,1[t\in]0,1[t∈]0,1[ (see Figure 14.4, panels 3 and 4), i.e.

∀ t∈]0,1[,f((1−t)x+ty)<(1−t)f(x)+tf(y).(14.6)\forall \,t \in ]0,1[, \quad f((1-t)x + t y) < (1-t)f(x) + t f(y). \tag{14.6}∀t∈]0,1[,f((1−t)x+ty)<(1−t)f(x)+tf(y).(14.6)

A minimizer x⋆x^\starx⋆ is then unique if it exists. Otherwise, two minimizers x1⋆≠x2⋆x_1^\star \neq x_2^\starx1⋆​=x2⋆​ would satisfy f(x1⋆+x2⋆2)<f(x1⋆)f(\frac{x_1^\star+x_2^\star}{2}) < f(x_1^\star)f(2x1⋆​+x2⋆​​)<f(x1⋆​) by strict convexity, contradicting optimality.

Example 14.2 (Least squares)

For the quadratic loss function f(x)=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y∣ ⁣∣2f(x)=\frac{1}{2}|\!| Ax-y |\!|^2f(x)=21​∣∣Ax−y∣∣2, strict convexity is equivalent to ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A)=\{0\}ker(A)={0}. Its Hessian is ∂2f(x)=A⊤A\partial^2 f(x)=A^\top A∂2f(x)=A⊤A, which is positive definite exactly when AAA is injective, since ⟨A⊤Az, z⟩=∣ ⁣∣Az∣ ⁣∣2\langle A^\top A z,\,z\rangle=|\!| Az |\!|^2⟨A⊤Az,z⟩=∣∣Az∣∣2. Positive definiteness implies strict convexity. Conversely, a nonzero vector in ker⁡(A)\ker(A)ker(A) gives a line along which fff is constant, ruling out strict convexity.

14.2.3 Convex Sets¶

A set Ω⊂Rp\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^pΩ⊂Rp is convex if every pair (x,y)∈Ω2(x,y) \in \Omega^2(x,y)∈Ω2 satisfies (1−t)x+ty∈Ω(1-t)x + t y \in \Omega(1−t)x+ty∈Ω for all t∈[0,1]t \in [0,1]t∈[0,1].

A function fff is convex exactly when its epigraph epi(f):={(x,t)∈Rp+1  ;  t⩾f(x)}\text{epi}(f) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^{p+1} \;;\; t \geqslant f(x) \right\}epi(f):={(x,t)∈Rp+1;t⩾f(x)} is a convex set.

Remark 14.3 (Convexity of the minimizer set)

A minimizer x⋆x^\starx⋆ need not be unique; see Figure 14.3.

For convex fff, the set argmin(f)\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}(f)argmin(f) is itself convex.

Indeed, if x1⋆x_1^\starx1⋆​ and x2⋆x_2^\starx2⋆​ are minimizers, so that in particular f(x1⋆)=f(x2⋆)=min⁡(f)f(x_1^\star)=f(x_2^\star)=\min(f)f(x1⋆​)=f(x2⋆​)=min(f), then f((1−t)x1⋆+tx2⋆)⩽(1−t)f(x1⋆)+tf(x2⋆)=f(x1⋆)=min⁡(f)f( (1-t)x_1^\star + t x_2^\star ) \leqslant(1-t) f(x_1^\star) + t f(x_2^\star) = f(x_1^\star) = \min(f)f((1−t)x1⋆​+tx2⋆​)⩽(1−t)f(x1⋆​)+tf(x2⋆​)=f(x1⋆​)=min(f), so that (1−t)x1⋆+tx2⋆(1-t)x_1^\star + t x_2^\star(1−t)x1⋆​+tx2⋆​ is itself a minimizer. 14.3 Derivative and gradient¶

14.3.1 Gradient¶

Figure 14.6. The gradient as a vector field.

When all coordinate derivatives of fff exist, define

∇f(x):=(∂f(x)∂x1,…,∂f(x)∂xp)⊤∈Rp\nabla f(x) \mathrel{:=}\left( \frac{ \partial f(x)}{\partial x_1} , \ldots, \frac{ \partial f(x)}{\partial x_p} \right)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^p∇f(x):=(∂x1​∂f(x)​,…,∂xp​∂f(x)​)⊤∈Rp

as the gradient vector. The map ∇f:Rp→Rp\nabla f : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^p∇f:Rp→Rp is a vector field, and its coordinate derivatives are defined by

∂f(x)∂xk:=lim⁡η→0f(x+ηδk)−f(x)η\frac{ \partial f(x)}{\partial x_k} \mathrel{:=}\lim_{\eta \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\eta \delta_k)-f(x)}{\eta}∂xk​∂f(x)​:=η→0lim​ηf(x+ηδk​)−f(x)​

where δk=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0)⊤∈Rp\delta_k=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^pδk​=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0)⊤∈Rp is the kkkth canonical basis vector.

Existence of the coordinate derivatives, hence of ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x), does not imply differentiability of fff. Differentiability of fff at xxx requires

f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨ε, ∇f(x)⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣).(14.7)f(x+\varepsilon) = f(x) + \langle \varepsilon,\,\nabla f(x)\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|). \tag{14.7}f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨ε,∇f(x)⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣).(14.7)

The remainder notation R(ε)=o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣)R(\varepsilon) = o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|)R(ε)=o(∣∣ε∣∣) means decay faster than the perturbation ε\varepsilonε as it tends to 0: R(ε)∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣→0\frac{R(\varepsilon)}{|\!| \varepsilon |\!|} \rightarrow 0∣∣ε∣∣R(ε)​→0 as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0ε→0. Coordinate derivatives concern the behavior of fff along the axes, whereas differentiability requires the expansion for every sequence ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0ε→0.

For example, f(x)=2x1x2(x1+x2)x12+x22f(x)=\frac{2 x_1 x_2 (x_1+x_2)}{x_1^2+x_2^2}f(x)=x12​+x22​2x1​x2​(x1​+x2​)​ with f(0)=0f(0)=0f(0)=0 has both coordinate derivatives equal to zero at the origin. Yet f(t,t)=2tf(t,t)=2tf(t,t)=2t, so the linear expansion with zero gradient fails.

The vector ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x) is uniquely determined by (14.7). To prove differentiability of fff and compute ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x), it therefore suffices to establish an expansion

f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨ε, g⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣),f(x+\varepsilon) = f(x) + \langle \varepsilon,\,g\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|),f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨ε,g⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣),

which identifies ∇f(x)=g\nabla f(x)=g∇f(x)=g.

For differentiable functions, convexity is equivalent to the graph lying above every tangent affine function.

Proposition 14.4

If fff is differentiable, then

f convex⇔∀(x,x′), f(x)⩾f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩.f \text{ convex} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad \forall (x,x'), \: f(x) \geqslant f(x') + \langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle.f convex⇔∀(x,x′),f(x)⩾f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩.
Proof

One can write the convexity condition as

f((1−t)x+tx′)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(x′)⟹f(x+t(x′−x))−f(x)t⩽f(x′)−f(x)f((1-t)x+tx') \leqslant(1-t) f(x) + t f(x') \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{ f( x + t (x'-x) ) - f(x) }{t} \leqslant f(x')-f(x)f((1−t)x+tx′)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(x′)⟹tf(x+t(x′−x))−f(x)​⩽f(x′)−f(x)

hence, taking the limit t→0t \rightarrow 0t→0 one obtains

⟨∇f(x), x′−x⟩⩽f(x′)−f(x).\langle \nabla f(x),\,x'-x\rangle \leqslant f(x')-f(x).⟨∇f(x),x′−x⟩⩽f(x′)−f(x).

Conversely, set xt:=(1−t)x+tx′x_t\mathrel{:=}(1-t)x+tx'xt​:=(1−t)x+tx′. Apply the supporting-affine-function inequality at xtx_txt​ to xxx and x′x'x′:

f(x)⩾f(xt)+⟨∇f(xt), x−xt⟩=f(xt)+t⟨∇f(xt), x−x′⟩f(x′)⩾f(xt)+⟨∇f(xt), x′−xt⟩=f(xt)−(1−t)⟨∇f(xt), x−x′⟩,\begin{aligned} f(x) & \geqslant f(x_t) + \langle \nabla f(x_t),\,x-x_t\rangle =f(x_t)+t\langle \nabla f(x_t),\,x-x'\rangle \\ f(x') & \geqslant f(x_t) + \langle \nabla f(x_t),\,x'-x_t\rangle =f(x_t)-(1-t)\langle \nabla f(x_t),\,x-x'\rangle, \end{aligned}f(x)f(x′)​⩾f(xt​)+⟨∇f(xt​),x−xt​⟩=f(xt​)+t⟨∇f(xt​),x−x′⟩⩾f(xt​)+⟨∇f(xt​),x′−xt​⟩=f(xt​)−(1−t)⟨∇f(xt​),x−x′⟩,​

Multiplying the first inequality by 1−t1-t1−t and the second by ttt, then adding, gives

(1−t)f(x)+tf(x′)⩾f(xt).(1-t)f(x)+t f(x') \geqslant f(x_t).(1−t)f(x)+tf(x′)⩾f(xt​).

14.3.2 First Order Conditions¶

A vanishing gradient is necessary for local optimality, and will also guide the algorithms developed below.

Proposition 14.5

If fff is differentiable and x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a local minimizer, meaning that f(x⋆)⩽f(x)f(x^\star)\leqslant f(x)f(x⋆)⩽f(x) throughout some neighborhood of x⋆x^\starx⋆, then

∇f(x⋆)=0.\nabla f(x^\star) = 0.∇f(x⋆)=0.
Proof

Fix a direction uuu and let ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow0ε↓0. Local optimality and differentiability give

f(x⋆)⩽f(x⋆+εu)=f(x⋆)+ε⟨∇f(x⋆), u⟩+o(ε)⟹⟨∇f(x⋆), u⟩⩾o(1)⟹⟨∇f(x⋆), u⟩⩾0.f(x^\star) \leqslant f(x^\star+\varepsilon u) = f(x^\star) + \varepsilon\langle \nabla f(x^\star),\,u\rangle + o(\varepsilon) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \langle \nabla f(x^\star),\,u\rangle \geqslant o(1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \langle \nabla f(x^\star),\,u\rangle \geqslant 0.f(x⋆)⩽f(x⋆+εu)=f(x⋆)+ε⟨∇f(x⋆),u⟩+o(ε)⟹⟨∇f(x⋆),u⟩⩾o(1)⟹⟨∇f(x⋆),u⟩⩾0.

So applying this for uuu and −u-u−u in the previous equation shows that ⟨∇f(x⋆), u⟩=0\langle \nabla f(x^\star),\,u\rangle=0⟨∇f(x⋆),u⟩=0 for all uuu, and hence ∇f(x⋆)=0\nabla f(x^\star)=0∇f(x⋆)=0.

Note that the converse is not true in general, since one might have ∇f(x)=0\nabla f(x)=0∇f(x)=0 but xxx is not a local minimum. For instance x=0x=0x=0 for f(x)=−x2f(x)=-x^2f(x)=−x2 (here xxx is a maximizer) or f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3f(x)=x3 (here xxx is neither a maximizer nor a minimizer; it is a stationary inflection point), see Fig. 14.7.

Stationarity alone therefore neither certifies a local minimum nor guarantees convergence of a numerical method to that point. Both depend on the local geometry.

Convexity of fff makes stationarity sufficient as well as necessary.

Figure 14.7. Local extrema (panel 1), a stationary inflection point (panel 2), and a global minimizer (panel 3).

Proposition 14.6

If fff is convex and x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a local minimizer, then x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a global minimizer. If fff is differentiable and convex,

x⋆∈argminx  f(x)⟺∇f(x⋆)=0.x^\star \in \underset{x}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; f(x) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nabla f(x^\star)=0.x⋆∈xargmin​f(x)⟺∇f(x⋆)=0.
Proof

Fix xxx and choose 0<t<10<t<10<t<1 so that tx+(1−t)x⋆tx+(1-t)x^\startx+(1−t)x⋆ lies in the neighborhood where x⋆x^\starx⋆ is minimal. Local optimality and convexity then give

f(x⋆)⩽f(tx+(1−t)x⋆)⩽tf(x)+(1−t)f(x⋆)⟹f(x⋆)⩽f(x)f(x^\star) \leqslant f(tx + (1-t)x^\star) \leqslant t f(x) + (1-t) f(x^\star) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x^\star) \leqslant f(x)f(x⋆)⩽f(tx+(1−t)x⋆)⩽tf(x)+(1−t)f(x⋆)⟹f(x⋆)⩽f(x)

proving that x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a global minimizer.

For the second part, we already saw in Proposition 14.5 the ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ implication. We assume that ∇f(x⋆)=0\nabla f(x^\star)=0∇f(x⋆)=0. Since the graph of fff is above its tangent by convexity (as stated in Proposition 14.4),

f(x)⩾f(x⋆)+⟨∇f(x⋆), x−x⋆⟩=f(x⋆).f(x) \geqslant f(x^\star) + \langle \nabla f(x^\star),\,x-x^\star\rangle = f(x^\star).f(x)⩾f(x⋆)+⟨∇f(x⋆),x−x⋆⟩=f(x⋆).

For a differentiable convex objective, minimization is therefore equivalent to solving ∇f(x)=0\nabla f(x)=0∇f(x)=0, a system of ppp equations in ppp unknowns.

An explicit solution is often unavailable, but the equation still characterizes the minimizers x⋆x^\starx⋆.

14.3.3 Least Squares¶

The gradient of the least-squares objective (14.3) follows by expanding the squared norm:

f(x+ε)=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y+Aε∣ ⁣∣2=12∣ ⁣∣Ax−y∣ ⁣∣2+⟨Ax−y, Aε⟩+12∣ ⁣∣Aε∣ ⁣∣2=f(x)+⟨ε, A⊤(Ax−y)⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣).\begin{aligned} f(x+\varepsilon) &= \frac{1}{2}|\!| Ax-y+A\varepsilon |\!|^2 = \frac12|\!| Ax-y |\!|^2+\langle Ax-y,\,A\varepsilon\rangle + \frac{1}{2}|\!| A\varepsilon |\!|^2 \\ &=f(x) + \langle \varepsilon,\,A^\top(Ax-y)\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|). \end{aligned}f(x+ε)​=21​∣∣Ax−y+Aε∣∣2=21​∣∣Ax−y∣∣2+⟨Ax−y,Aε⟩+21​∣∣Aε∣∣2=f(x)+⟨ε,A⊤(Ax−y)⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣).​

We used ∣ ⁣∣Aε∣ ⁣∣2=o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣)|\!| A\varepsilon |\!|^2 = o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|)∣∣Aε∣∣2=o(∣∣ε∣∣) and the transpose A⊤A^\topA⊤.

The transpose exchanges rows and columns, A⊤=(Aj,i)i=1,…,nj=1,…,pA^\top = (A_{j,i})_{i=1,\ldots,n}^{j=1,\ldots,p}A⊤=(Aj,i​)i=1,…,nj=1,…,p​. Its essential role in gradient calculations is the adjoint identity

∀ (u,v)∈Rp×Rn,⟨Au, v⟩Rn=⟨u, A⊤v⟩Rp.\forall \,(u,v) \in \mathbb{R}^{p} \times \mathbb{R}^n, \quad \langle A u,\,v\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^n} = \langle u,\,A^\top v\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^p}.∀(u,v)∈Rp×Rn,⟨Au,v⟩Rn​=⟨u,A⊤v⟩Rp​.

Computing gradients of functions involving linear operators requires such a transposition step.

This computation shows that

∇f(x)=A⊤(Ax−y).(14.8)\nabla f(x) = A^\top (A x - y). \tag{14.8}∇f(x)=A⊤(Ax−y).(14.8)

Hence every minimizer x⋆x^\starx⋆ of f(x)f(x)f(x) satisfies the normal equations (A⊤A)x⋆=A⊤y(A^\top A) x^\star = A^\top y(A⊤A)x⋆=A⊤y.

If A⋆A∈Rp×pA^\star A \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}A⋆A∈Rp×p is invertible, then fff has a single minimizer, namely

x⋆=(A⊤A)−1A⊤y.(14.9)x^\star = (A^\top A)^{-1} A^\top y. \tag{14.9}x⋆=(A⊤A)−1A⊤y.(14.9)

Thus x⋆x^\starx⋆ depends linearly on yyy. The operator (A⊤A)−1A⋆(A^\top A)^{-1} A^\star(A⊤A)−1A⋆ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of AAA; an ordinary inverse is unavailable when p≠np \neq np=n.

The condition that A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is invertible is equivalent to ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A)=\{0\}ker(A)={0}, since

A⊤Ax=0⟹∣ ⁣∣Ax∣ ⁣∣2=⟨A⊤Ax, x⟩=0⟹Ax=0.A^\top A x = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad|\!| Ax |\!|^2 = \langle A^\top A x,\,x\rangle = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A x= 0.A⊤Ax=0⟹∣∣Ax∣∣2=⟨A⊤Ax,x⟩=0⟹Ax=0.

When n<pn<pn<p, the system is underdetermined and injectivity is impossible. If n⩾pn\geqslant pn⩾p and the entries of AAA have a joint density, then ker⁡(A)={0}\ker(A)=\{0\}ker(A)={0} almost surely. In general, injectivity is equivalent to the feature vectors aia_iai​ spanning Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp.

14.3.6 Chain Rule¶

More generally, for f(x)=g(Bx)f(x) = g(Bx)f(x)=g(Bx) with B∈Rq×pB \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}B∈Rq×p and g:Rq→Rg : \mathbb{R}^q \rightarrow \mathbb{R}g:Rq→R,

f(x+ε)=g(Bx+Bε)=g(Bx)+⟨∇g(Bx), Bε⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣Bε∣ ⁣∣)=f(x)+⟨ε, B⊤∇g(Bx)⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣),f(x+\varepsilon) = g(Bx + B\varepsilon) = g(Bx) + \langle \nabla g(Bx),\,B \varepsilon\rangle + o(|\!| B \varepsilon |\!|) = f(x) + \langle \varepsilon,\,B^\top \nabla g(Bx)\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|),f(x+ε)=g(Bx+Bε)=g(Bx)+⟨∇g(Bx),Bε⟩+o(∣∣Bε∣∣)=f(x)+⟨ε,B⊤∇g(Bx)⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣),

which shows that

∇(g∘B)=B⊤∘∇g∘B(14.11)\nabla ( g \circ B ) = B^\top \circ \nabla g \circ B \tag{14.11}∇(g∘B)=B⊤∘∇g∘B(14.11)

where “∘” denotes the composition of functions.

Nonlinear compositions require the differential. For F:Rp→RqF : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^qF:Rp→Rq, its differential at xxx is the linear map ∂F(x):Rp→Rq\partial F(x) : \mathbb{R}^{p} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^q∂F(x):Rp→Rq. We represent it by its Jacobian matrix, also denoted ∂F(x)\partial F(x)∂F(x), with dimensions ∂F(x)∈Rq×p\partial F(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}∂F(x)∈Rq×p.

Writing F(x)=(F1(x),…,Fq(x))F(x)=(F_1(x), \ldots, F_q(x))F(x)=(F1​(x),…,Fq​(x)), the Jacobian entries are

∀ (i,j)∈{1,…,q}×{1,…,p},[∂F(x)]i,j:=∂Fi(x)∂xj.\forall \,(i,j) \in \{1,\ldots,q\} \times \{1,\ldots,p\}, \quad [ \partial F(x) ]_{i,j} \mathrel{:=}\frac{\partial F_i(x)}{\partial x_j}.∀(i,j)∈{1,…,q}×{1,…,p},[∂F(x)]i,j​:=∂xj​∂Fi​(x)​.

The map FFF is differentiable at xxx when it admits the expansion

F(x+ε)=F(x)+[∂F(x)](ε)+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣).(14.12)F(x+\varepsilon) = F(x) + [\partial F(x)](\varepsilon) + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|). \tag{14.12}F(x+ε)=F(x)+[∂F(x)](ε)+o(∣∣ε∣∣).(14.12)

Here [∂F(x)](ε)[\partial F(x)](\varepsilon)[∂F(x)](ε) denotes matrix-vector multiplication. The matrix in this expansion is unique, so the expansion can also be used to compute the differential.

For the special case q=1q=1q=1, i.e. if f:Rp→Rf : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:Rp→R, then the differential ∂f(x)∈R1×p\partial f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times p}∂f(x)∈R1×p and the gradient ∇f(x)∈Rp×1\nabla f(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}∇f(x)∈Rp×1 are linked by equating the Taylor expansions (14.12) and (14.7)

∀ ε∈Rp,[∂f(x)](ε)=⟨∇f(x), ε⟩⇔∂f(x)=∇f(x)⊤.\forall \,\varepsilon\in \mathbb{R}^p, \quad [\partial f(x)](\varepsilon) = \langle \nabla f(x),\,\varepsilon\rangle \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad \partial f(x)=\nabla f(x)^\top.∀ε∈Rp,[∂f(x)](ε)=⟨∇f(x),ε⟩⇔∂f(x)=∇f(x)⊤.

The differential satisfies the following chain rule

∂(G∘H)(x)=[∂G(H(x))]×[∂H(x)]\partial( G \circ H)(x) = [\partial G(H(x))] \times [\partial H(x)]∂(G∘H)(x)=[∂G(H(x))]×[∂H(x)]

where “×\times×” is the matrix product. For instance, if H:Rp→RqH : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^qH:Rp→Rq and G=g:Rq↦RG = g : \mathbb{R}^q \mapsto \mathbb{R}G=g:Rq↦R, then f=g∘H:Rp→Rf = g \circ H : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f=g∘H:Rp→R and one can compute its gradient as follows

∇f(x)=(∂f(x))⊤=([∂g(H(x))]×[∂H(x)])⊤=[∂H(x)]⊤×[∂g(H(x))]⊤=[∂H(x)]⊤×∇g(H(x)).\nabla f(x) = (\partial f(x))^\top = \left( [\partial g(H(x))] \times [\partial H(x)] \right)^\top = [\partial H(x)]^\top \times [\partial g(H(x))]^\top = [\partial H(x)]^\top \times \nabla g(H(x)).∇f(x)=(∂f(x))⊤=([∂g(H(x))]×[∂H(x)])⊤=[∂H(x)]⊤×[∂g(H(x))]⊤=[∂H(x)]⊤×∇g(H(x)).

When H(x)=BxH(x)=BxH(x)=Bx is linear, one recovers formula (14.11).

14.4 Gradient Descent Algorithm¶

14.4.1 Steepest Descent Direction¶

The Taylor expansion (14.7) approximates fff near xxx by an affine function:

f(z)=Tx(z)+o(∣ ⁣∣x−z∣ ⁣∣)whereTx(z):=f(x)+⟨∇f(x), z−x⟩,f(z) = T_x(z) + o(|\!| x-z |\!|) \quad \text{where} \quad T_x(z) \mathrel{:=}f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x),\,z-x\rangle,f(z)=Tx​(z)+o(∣∣x−z∣∣)whereTx​(z):=f(x)+⟨∇f(x),z−x⟩,

If fff is differentiable at xxx, one has

If ∇f(x)=0\nabla f(x)=0∇f(x)=0, then xxx is stationary and is a global minimizer when fff is convex. Otherwise, for sufficiently small τ\tauτ,

f(x−τ∇f(x))<f(x)f(x-\tau \nabla f(x)) < f(x)f(x−τ∇f(x))<f(x)

so the step from xxx to x−τ∇f(x)x-\tau \nabla f(x)x−τ∇f(x) decreases the objective.

Remark 14.7 (Orthogonality to level sets)

A level set of fff contains points with the same value of fff. For s∈Rs \in \mathbb{R}s∈R, define

Ls:={x  ;  f(x)=s}.\mathcal{L}_s \mathrel{:=} \left\{ x \;;\; f(x)=s \right\} .Ls​:={x;f(x)=s}.

Take a smooth curve through xxx in Ls\mathcal{L}_sLs​, parameterized by t∈R↦c(t)t \in \mathbb{R}\mapsto c(t)t∈R↦c(t) with c(0)=xc(0)=xc(0)=x.

i.e. h′(0)=⟨c′(0), ∇f(x)⟩=0h'(0) = \langle c'(0),\,\nabla f(x)\rangle=0h′(0)=⟨c′(0),∇f(x)⟩=0, so that ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x) is orthogonal to the tangent c′(0)c'(0)c′(0) of the curve ccc, which lies in the tangent plane of Ls\mathcal{L}_sLs​ (as shown in Figure 14.9, panel 3). Since the curve ccc is arbitrary, the whole tangent plane is thus orthogonal to ∇f(x)\nabla f(x)∇f(x).

Remark 14.8 (Local optimal descent direction)

14.4.2 Gradient Descent¶

Starting from x0∈Rpx_0 \in \mathbb{R}^px0​∈Rp, gradient descent iterates

xk+1:=xk−τk∇f(xk)(14.13)x_{k+1} \mathrel{:=}x_k - \tau_k \nabla f(x_k) \tag{14.13}xk+1​:=xk​−τk​∇f(xk​)(14.13)

The parameter τk>0\tau_k>0τk​>0 is the step size, or learning rate. A sufficiently small τk\tau_kτk​ decreases fff at a nonstationary iterate. Choosing τk\tau_kτk​ balances stable descent against progress per step.

One may fix τk=τ\tau_k=\tauτk​=τ or adapt τk\tau_kτk​ at each iteration; see Figure 14.10.

Remark 14.9 (Greedy choice)

Exact line search chooses the best step along the current direction, although computing it can be expensive:

τk∈argminτ⩾0  h(τ):=f(xk−τ∇f(xk)).\tau_k\in\underset{\tau\geqslant 0}{\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}}\; h(\tau) \mathrel{:=}f(x_k-\tau \nabla f(x_k)).τk​∈τ⩾0argmin​h(τ):=f(xk​−τ∇f(xk​)).

The line-search objective h(τ)h(\tau)h(τ) is scalar. Its derivative follows from a Taylor expansion of hhh:

h(τ+δ)=f(xk−τ∇f(xk)−δ∇f(xk))=f(xk−τ∇f(xk))−δ⟨∇f(xk−τ∇f(xk)), ∇f(xk)⟩+o(δ).h(\tau+\delta) = f(x_k-\tau \nabla f(x_k) - \delta\nabla f(x_k)) = f(x_k-\tau\nabla f(x_k))-\delta\langle \nabla f(x_k-\tau \nabla f(x_k)),\, \nabla f(x_k)\rangle + o(\delta).h(τ+δ)=f(xk​−τ∇f(xk​)−δ∇f(xk​))=f(xk​−τ∇f(xk​))−δ⟨∇f(xk​−τ∇f(xk​)),∇f(xk​)⟩+o(δ).

Note that at τ=τk\tau=\tau_kτ=τk​, ∇f(xk−τ∇f(xk))=∇f(xk+1)\nabla f(x_k-\tau \nabla f(x_k))=\nabla f(x_{k+1})∇f(xk​−τ∇f(xk​))=∇f(xk+1​) by definition of xk+1x_{k+1}xk+1​ in (14.13).

If the current gradient is nonzero and the minimum is attained, an optimal step satisfies τk>0\tau_k>0τk​>0, since small positive steps decrease fff. The first-order condition is therefore

h′(τk)=−⟨∇f(xk), ∇f(xk+1)⟩=0.h'(\tau_k) = - \langle \nabla f(x_k),\,\nabla f(x_{k+1})\rangle = 0.h′(τk​)=−⟨∇f(xk​),∇f(xk+1​)⟩=0.

Thus successive gradients, and hence successive descent directions, are orthogonal; see Figure 14.10.

Remark 14.10 (Armijo rule)

Instead of finding the optimal τ\tauτ, Armijo backtracking seeks an admissible τ\tauτ that produces sufficient decrease.

Given 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1 (values below 1/21/21/2 are customary, especially for Newton-type methods), one considers a τ\tauτ to be valid for a descent direction dkd_kdk​ (for instance dk=−∇f(xk)d_k=-\nabla f(x_k)dk​=−∇f(xk​)) if it satisfies

f(xk+τdk)⩽f(xk)+ατ⟨dk, ∇f(xk)⟩(14.14)f(x_k+\tau d_k) \leqslant f(x_k) + \alpha\tau \langle d_k,\,\nabla f(x_k)\rangle \tag{14.14}f(xk​+τdk​)⩽f(xk​)+ατ⟨dk​,∇f(xk​)⟩(14.14)

For small τ\tauτ, one has f(xk+τdk)=f(xk)+τ⟨dk, ∇f(xk)⟩+o(τ)f(x_k+\tau d_k) = f(x_k)+\tau\langle d_k,\,\nabla f(x_k)\rangle+o(\tau)f(xk​+τdk​)=f(xk​)+τ⟨dk​,∇f(xk​)⟩+o(τ), so that, assuming dkd_kdk​ is a valid descent direction (i.e ⟨dk, ∇f(xk)⟩<0\langle d_k,\,\nabla f(x_k)\rangle<0⟨dk​,∇f(xk​)⟩<0), condition (14.14) will always be satisfied for τ\tauτ small enough (if fff is convex, the set of allowable τ\tauτ is of the form [0,τmax⁡][0,\tau_{\max}][0,τmax​]).

Start from a positive trial step and repeatedly reduce it by τ←βτ\tau\leftarrow\beta\tauτ←βτ, with 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1, until (14.14) holds.

This procedure is called backtracking line search.

14.5 Convergence Analysis¶

14.5.1 Quadratic Case¶

Convergence analysis for the quadratic case.

We first analyze gradient descent for the quadratic objective

We also use ε\varepsilonε below for this inverse condition number. The condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, and its minimum value is 1, attained by orthogonal matrices.

The geometric decay O(ρk)O(\rho^k)O(ρk) in (14.15) is called linear convergence in optimization. The bound is global because it holds for every kkk, rather than only sufficiently large kkk.

The spectral argument also relies on the quadratic structure. We therefore give a different analysis that provides a sublinear bound on the objective value.

14.5.2 General Case¶

We now extend the convergence analysis to general smooth convex functions.

The Hessian replaces the constant matrix CCC of a quadratic objective.

Hessian.

For a twice continuously differentiable function, the Hessian matrix is

(∂2f)(x)=(∂2f(x)∂xi∂xj)1⩽i,j⩽p∈Rp×p.(\partial^2 f)(x) = \left( \frac{\partial^2 f(x)}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} \right)_{1 \leqslant i,j \leqslant p} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}.(∂2f)(x)=(∂xi​∂xj​∂2f(x)​)1⩽i,j⩽p​∈Rp×p.

Each entry differentiates the iiith component of the gradient with respect to the jjjth coordinate. Equality of mixed partial derivatives makes ∂2f(x)\partial^2 f(x)∂2f(x) symmetric.

Twice differentiability of fff at xxx implies the Taylor expansion

f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x), ε⟩+12⟨∂2f(x)ε, ε⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣2).(14.18)f(x+\varepsilon) = f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x),\,\varepsilon\rangle + \frac{1}{2} \langle \partial^2 f(x) \varepsilon,\,\varepsilon\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|^2). \tag{14.18}f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x),ε⟩+21​⟨∂2f(x)ε,ε⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣2).(14.18)

Thus fff has a local quadratic approximation near xxx.

The Hessian is the unique symmetric matrix in this expansion. If an expansion has the form below with a symmetric matrix HHH,

f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x), ε⟩+12⟨Hε, ε⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣2).f(x+\varepsilon) = f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x),\,\varepsilon\rangle + \frac{1}{2} \langle H \varepsilon,\,\varepsilon\rangle + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|^2).f(x+ε)=f(x)+⟨∇f(x),ε⟩+21​⟨Hε,ε⟩+o(∣∣ε∣∣2).

comparison with (14.18) identifies ∂2f(x)=H\partial^2 f(x)=H∂2f(x)=H, avoiding separate computation of all p2p^2p2 partial derivatives.

Equivalently, differentiate the gradient:

∇f(x+ε)=∇f(x)+[∂2f(x)](ε)+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣)\nabla f(x+\varepsilon) = \nabla f(x) + [\partial^2 f(x)](\varepsilon) + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|)∇f(x+ε)=∇f(x)+[∂2f(x)](ε)+o(∣∣ε∣∣)

where [∂2f(x)](ε)∈Rp[\partial^2 f(x)](\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{R}^p[∂2f(x)](ε)∈Rp is the product of the Hessian ∂2f(x)\partial^2 f(x)∂2f(x) with ε\varepsilonε.

A twice differentiable function fff on Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp is convex exactly when, at every xxx, the Hessian ∂2f(x)\partial^2 f(x)∂2f(x) is positive semidefinite.

Positive definiteness everywhere implies strict convexity of fff, but is not necessary: x4x^4x4 is strictly convex on R\mathbb{R}R although its second derivative vanishes at x=0x=0x=0.

For a quadratic objective f(x)=12⟨Cx, x⟩−⟨x, u⟩f(x)=\frac12\langle Cx,\,x\rangle-\langle x,\,u\ranglef(x)=21​⟨Cx,x⟩−⟨x,u⟩, the gradient ∇f(x)=Cx−u\nabla f(x) = Cx-u∇f(x)=Cx−u gives the constant Hessian ∂2f(x)=C\partial^2 f(x) = C∂2f(x)=C.

For the classification function, one has

∇f(x)=−A⊤diag(y)∇L(−diag(y)Ax).\nabla f(x) = -A^\top \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) \nabla L( -\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) Ax).∇f(x)=−A⊤diag(y)∇L(−diag(y)Ax).

and thus

∇f(x+ε)=−A⊤diag(y)∇L(−diag(y)Ax−diag(y)Aε)=∇f(x)−A⊤diag(y)[∂2L(−diag(y)Ax)](−diag(y)Aε)+o(∣ ⁣∣ε∣ ⁣∣)\begin{aligned} \nabla f(x+\varepsilon) &= -A^\top \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) \nabla L( -\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) Ax-\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y)A\varepsilon) \\ &= \nabla f(x) -A^\top \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) [\partial^2 L( -\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) Ax)]( -\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) A\varepsilon) + o(|\!| \varepsilon |\!|) \end{aligned}∇f(x+ε)​=−A⊤diag(y)∇L(−diag(y)Ax−diag(y)Aε)=∇f(x)−A⊤diag(y)[∂2L(−diag(y)Ax)](−diag(y)Aε)+o(∣∣ε∣∣)​

Since ∇L(u)=(ℓ′(ui))\nabla L(u) = (\ell'(u_i))∇L(u)=(ℓ′(ui​)) one has ∂2L(u)=diag(ℓ′′(ui))\partial^2 L(u)=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\ell''(u_i))∂2L(u)=diag(ℓ′′(ui​)). This means that

∂2f(x)=A⊤diag(y)×diag(ℓ′′(−diag(y)Ax))×diag(y)A.\partial^2 f(x) = A^\top \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) \times \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}( \ell''(-\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) Ax) ) \times \mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(y) A.∂2f(x)=A⊤diag(y)×diag(ℓ′′(−diag(y)Ax))×diag(y)A.

This matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite when ℓ\ellℓ is convex, because ℓ′′\ell''ℓ′′ is nonnegative.

Remark 14.13 (Second order optimality condition)

The Hessian can classify a stationary point x⋆x^\starx⋆ with ∇f(x⋆)=0\nabla f(x^\star)=0∇f(x⋆)=0. If ∂2f(x⋆)\partial^2 f(x^\star)∂2f(x⋆) is positive definite, then x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a strict local minimizer.

Positive semidefiniteness of ∂2f(x⋆)\partial^2 f(x^\star)∂2f(x⋆) alone does not classify the point; for example, x3x^3x3 on R\mathbb{R}R has a vanishing Hessian at its stationary inflection point.

Conversely, if x⋆x^\starx⋆ is a local minimum, then ∂2f(x⋆)\partial^2 f(x^\star)∂2f(x⋆) is positive semidefinite.

Remark 14.14 (Second order algorithms)

The Hessian also yields second-order methods such as Newton’s method. These can converge faster locally than gradient descent, at a greater cost per iteration. A variable-metric gradient step has the form

xk+1=xk−Hk∇f(xk)x_{k+1} = x_k - H_k \nabla f(x_k)xk+1​=xk​−Hk​∇f(xk​)

where Hk∈Rp×pH_k \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}Hk​∈Rp×p is symmetric positive definite. Gradient descent uses Hk=τkIdpH_k=\tau_k \mathrm{Id}_pHk​=τk​Idp​; Newton’s method uses Hk=[∂2f(xk)]−1H_k=[\partial^2 f(x_k)]^{-1}Hk​=[∂2f(xk​)]−1 when the Hessian is positive definite.

Note that

f(xk+1)=f(xk)−⟨Hk∇f(xk), ∇f(xk)⟩+o(∣ ⁣∣Hk∇f(xk)∣ ⁣∣).f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)-\langle H_k \nabla f(x_k),\,\nabla f(x_k)\rangle + o(|\!| H_k \nabla f(x_k) |\!|).f(xk+1​)=f(xk​)−⟨Hk​∇f(xk​),∇f(xk​)⟩+o(∣∣Hk​∇f(xk​)∣∣).

Positive definiteness of HkH_kHk​ ensures that, if xkx_kxk​ is nonstationary with ∇f(xk)≠0\nabla f(x_k)\neq0∇f(xk​)=0, then ⟨Hk∇f(xk), ∇f(xk)⟩>0\langle H_k \nabla f(x_k),\,\nabla f(x_k)\rangle>0⟨Hk​∇f(xk​),∇f(xk​)⟩>0.

Scaling HkH_kHk​ sufficiently small therefore guarantees descent, f(xk+1)<f(xk)f(x_{k+1}) < f(x_k)f(xk+1​)<f(xk​).

We do not develop second-order algorithms further here.

For convergence analysis, uniform Hessian bounds play the role of the spectral bounds on CCC in the quadratic case. We require these bounds on ∂2f(x)\partial^2 f(x)∂2f(x) at every xxx.

Integrating these local bounds yields global inequalities that support an analysis similar to the quadratic one.

Smoothness and strong convexity.

Figure 14.12. Quadratic upper and lower bounds for a smooth strongly convex function.

For L>0L>0L>0, quantify the smoothness of fff by requiring an LLL-Lipschitz gradient:

∀ (x,x′)∈(Rp)2,∣ ⁣∣∇f(x)−∇f(x′)∣ ⁣∣⩽L∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣.(RL)\forall \,(x,x') \in (\mathbb{R}^p)^2, \quad |\!| \nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x') |\!| \leqslant L |\!| x-x' |\!|. \tag{$\mathcal{R}_L$}∀(x,x′)∈(Rp)2,∣∣∇f(x)−∇f(x′)∣∣⩽L∣∣x−x′∣∣.(RL​)

A linear convergence guarantee for the iterates follows from a uniform lower curvature bound. We impose this by assuming that fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex

∀ (x,x′)∈(Rp)2,⟨∇f(x)−∇f(x′), x−x′⟩⩾μ∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2.(Sμ)\forall \,(x,x')\in (\mathbb{R}^p)^2, \quad \langle \nabla f(x)-\nabla f(x'),\, x-x' \rangle \geqslant\mu |\!| x-x' |\!|^2. \tag{$\mathcal{S}_\mu$}∀(x,x′)∈(Rp)2,⟨∇f(x)−∇f(x′),x−x′⟩⩾μ∣∣x−x′∣∣2.(Sμ​)

For C2\mathcal{C}^2C2 functions, these conditions are equivalent to uniform Hessian bounds.

Proposition 14.15

Conditions (RL\mathcal {R}_LRL​) and (Sμ\mathcal {S}_\mu Sμ​) imply

∀ (x,x′),f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩+μ2∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2⩽f(x)⩽f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′), x−x′⟩+L2∣ ⁣∣x−x′∣ ⁣∣2.(14.19)\forall \,(x,x'), \quad f(x')+\langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2 \leqslant f(x) \leqslant f(x')+\langle \nabla f(x'),\,x-x'\rangle+\frac{L}{2}|\!| x-x' |\!|^2. \tag{14.19}∀(x,x′),f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩+2μ​∣∣x−x′∣∣2⩽f(x)⩽f(x′)+⟨∇f(x′),x−x′⟩+2L​∣∣x−x′∣∣2.(14.19)

If fff is of class C2\mathcal{C}^2C2, conditions (RL\mathcal {R}_LRL​) and (Sμ\mathcal {S}_\mu Sμ​) are equivalent to

∀ x,μIdp⪯∂2f(x)⪯LIdp(14.20)\forall \,x, \quad \mu \mathrm{Id}_{p} \preceq \partial^2 f(x) \preceq L \mathrm{Id}_{p} \tag{14.20}∀x,μIdp​⪯∂2f(x)⪯LIdp​(14.20)

where ∂2f(x)∈Rp×p\partial^2 f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}∂2f(x)∈Rp×p is the Hessian and ⪯\preceq⪯ denotes the semidefinite order:

A⪯B⟺∀ u∈Rp,⟨Au, u⟩⩽⟨Bu, u⟩.A \preceq B \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall \,u\in\mathbb{R}^p,\quad\langle Au,\,u\rangle \leqslant\langle B u,\,u\rangle.A⪯B⟺∀u∈Rp,⟨Au,u⟩⩽⟨Bu,u⟩.

We prove (14.19), using Taylor expansion with integral remainder

f(x′)−f(x)=∫01⟨∇f(xt), x′−x⟩dt=⟨∇f(x), x′−x⟩+∫01⟨∇f(xt)−∇f(x), x′−x⟩dtf(x') - f(x) = \int_0^1 \langle \nabla f(x_t),\,x'-x\rangle \mathrm{d}t = \langle \nabla f(x),\,x'-x\rangle + \int_0^1 \langle \nabla f(x_t)-\nabla f(x),\,x'-x\rangle \mathrm{d}tf(x′)−f(x)=∫01​⟨∇f(xt​),x′−x⟩dt=⟨∇f(x),x′−x⟩+∫01​⟨∇f(xt​)−∇f(x),x′−x⟩dt

which gives the desired result since ∣ ⁣∣xt−x∣ ⁣∣2/t=t∣ ⁣∣x′−x∣ ⁣∣2|\!| x_t-x |\!|^2 / t = t |\!| x'-x |\!|^2∣∣xt​−x∣∣2/t=t∣∣x′−x∣∣2.

Equation (14.19) places the objective between a lower quadratic tangent model from strong convexity and an upper quadratic tangent model from smoothness.

Condition (14.20) places every eigenvalue of ∂2f(x)\partial^2 f(x)∂2f(x) in [μ,L][\mu,L][μ,L]. The upper bound is also equivalent to ∣ ⁣∣∂2f(x)∣ ⁣∣op⩽L|\!| \partial^2 f(x) |\!|_{\text{op}} \leqslant L∣∣∂2f(x)∣∣op​⩽L where ∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣op|\!| \cdot |\!|_{\text{op}}∣∣⋅∣∣op​ is the operator norm, i.e. the largest singular value.

In the special case of a quadratic function of the form 12⟨Cx, x⟩−⟨b, x⟩\frac12\langle Cx,\,x\rangle-\langle b,\,x\rangle21​⟨Cx,x⟩−⟨b,x⟩ (with CCC symmetric positive semidefinite), ∂2f(x)=C\partial^2 f(x)=C∂2f(x)=C is constant, so that [μ,L][\mu,L][μ,L] can be chosen to be the range of the eigenvalues of CCC.

Convergence analysis.

For a general smooth convex function, gradient descent admits a sublinear objective bound. Strong convexity gives a linear rate for the iterates. Other structural assumptions can also yield faster rates, but are outside this analysis.

Without strong convexity, the minimizer need not be unique.

If fff is convex, satisfies (RL\mathcal {R}_LRL​), and has a minimizer, assume there are constants τmin⁡,τmax⁡\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}τmin​,τmax​ such that

0<τmin⁡⩽τℓ⩽τmax⁡<2L,0 < \tau_{\min} \leqslant\tau_\ell \leqslant\tau_{\max} < \frac{2}{L},0<τmin​⩽τℓ​⩽τmax​<L2​,

then xkx_kxk​ converges to a solution x⋆x^\starx⋆ of (14.1) and there exists C>0C>0C>0 such that

If furthermore fff is μ\muμ-strongly convex, then there exists 0⩽ρ<10 \leqslant\rho < 10⩽ρ<1 such that ∣ ⁣∣xk−x⋆∣ ⁣∣⩽ρk∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣|\!| x_k-x^\star |\!| \leqslant\rho^k |\!| x_0-x^\star |\!|∣∣xk​−x⋆∣∣⩽ρk∣∣x0​−x⋆∣∣.

14.5.3 Acceleration¶

For a convex function with an LLL-Lipschitz gradient, ordinary gradient descent has a worst-case O(1/k)O(1/k)O(1/k) objective bound. Accelerated methods combine a gradient step with extrapolation. Starting from y0=x0y_0=x_0y0​=x0​ and 0<s⩽1/L0<s\leqslant 1/L0<s⩽1/L, one example is

xk+1=yk−s∇f(yk),yk+1=xk+1+βk(xk+1−xk),βk=kk+3.x_{k+1}=y_k-s\nabla f(y_k),\qquad y_{k+1}=x_{k+1}+\beta_k(x_{k+1}-x_k),\qquad \beta_k=\frac{k}{k+3}.xk+1​=yk​−s∇f(yk​),yk+1​=xk+1​+βk​(xk+1​−xk​),βk​=k+3k​.

This is a Nesterov-type scheme. It differs from the heavy-ball method, which evaluates the gradient at xkx_kxk​ and adds momentum to that step. The accelerated scheme satisfies

f(xk)−f(x⋆)=O(∣ ⁣∣x0−x⋆∣ ⁣∣2sk2).f(x_k)-f(x^\star)=O\left(\frac{|\!| x_0-x^\star |\!|^2}{s k^2}\right).f(xk​)−f(x⋆)=O(sk2∣∣x0​−x⋆∣∣2​).

This is a worst-case guarantee; it does not ensure that every individual trajectory is faster. If strong convexity is known, appropriately tuned acceleration or restart can give a linear rate.

A formal continuous-time limit explains the momentum schedule. Set τ=s\tau=\sqrt sτ=s​ and t=kτt=k\taut=kτ. Since βk−1=(k−1)/(k+2)\beta_{k-1}=(k-1)/(k+2)βk−1​=(k−1)/(k+2),

xk+1−2xk+xk−1τ2+3(k+2)τxk−xk−1τ+∇f(yk)=0.\frac{x_{k+1}-2x_k+x_{k-1}}{\tau^2} +\frac{3}{(k+2)\tau}\frac{x_k-x_{k-1}}{\tau} +\nabla f(y_k)=0.τ2xk+1​−2xk​+xk−1​​+(k+2)τ3​τxk​−xk−1​​+∇f(yk​)=0.

If the interpolated iterates converge smoothly as τ→0\tau\to0τ→0, the limit solves

x′′(t)+3tx′(t)+∇f(x(t))=0,x(0)=x0,x′(0)=0.x''(t)+\frac3t x'(t)+\nabla f(x(t))=0,\qquad x(0)=x_0,\quad x'(0)=0.x′′(t)+t3​x′(t)+∇f(x(t))=0,x(0)=x0​,x′(0)=0.

The term 3x′(t)/t3x'(t)/t3x′(t)/t is a time-dependent friction. Its decay permits inertial motion while retaining an accelerated energy bound. The coefficient 3 is not the only admissible choice: related dynamics with friction α/t\alpha/tα/t for α⩾3\alpha\geqslant 3α⩾3 also admit O(t−2)O(t^{-2})O(t−2) objective estimates under the usual convexity assumptions.
